name: Airbyte, Inc.
origin_detail: Founded Jan 2020 in San Francisco by Michel Tricot (CEO) and John Lafleur (COO), French founders in Y Combinator's Winter 2020 batch; pivoted from a marketing-data product during COVID-19; first open-source release late 2020
openness_notes: Launched fully MIT-licensed (2020). In Sep 2021 the core platform moved to the Elastic License v2 (source-available, not OSI); connectors stayed MIT. In Jun 2023 ELv2 was extended to some API, database and warehouse source connectors. The self-hosted version remains free to use; Cloud and Enterprise (extra security features) are the business. Rated 1 because the core is ELv2.

relicensing_events.outcome_note: Made to stop cloud providers reselling the platform; done months before a $150M Series B at a $1.5B valuation (Dec 2021); no significant fork found
Extended the source-available licence to selected API, database and warehouse source connectors

risk_events: 2021 and 2023 moves from MIT to ELv2 (source-available) for the core and some connectors
No new priced round found since the Dec 2021 $1.5B Series B (as of Apr 2025), a valuation set at the 2021 market peak
Larger competitors consolidating: Fivetran (valued $5.6B in 2021) and dbt Labs ($4.2B in 2022) agreed to merge in 2025
robustness: Large open community (20-25K Slack members; 170K+ deployments and 7K+ companies syncing daily as of Sep 2024; 22.4k GitHub stars) and MIT-licensed connectors that others can reuse, but the core platform is ELv2 and controlled by a single ~140-person VC-backed company. Shipped Airbyte 1.0 (Sep 2024) and 2.0 (Sep 2025), so it is still active.
physical_science_relevance: Low directly; used to move operational and SaaS data into warehouses. Its connector-catalog model is relevant to research data integration.
openness_effect_assessment: MIT licensing and a community connector catalog drove extremely fast adoption (zero to unicorn in under two years). Airbyte closed its core under ELv2 within ~18 months of launch, before rather than after scaling, which avoided a fork but turned it into a source-available vendor; it has since raised no disclosed new money, so the long-term value of the closing move is unproven.
key_takeaway: Airbyte is the fast-closing case in this group: born MIT in 2020, ELv2 by 2021, a $1.5B valuation the same year, and then a long gap without new priced funding while bigger rivals merged. Openness bought rapid adoption; restriction came early to fend off cloud resellers, and the company's fate now depends on monetizing the cloud product.
